1.text:
What Can the Sky Tell Us Without a Telescope?

Long before anyone built a telescope, people worked out a surprising amount just by looking up and paying attention. They figured out where north is, how far north they lived, when the seasons would change, when eclipses could happen, and even why the ocean rises and falls twice a day.

That's the plan for this deck. We'll start with the giant "ball" of sky that seems to spin around us every day. Then we'll follow the Sun's path through the year, meet a slow wobble in Earth's axis, and finish with the Moon: its phases, its eclipses, and its pull on the oceans.

See the little drawing in the corner? That's the Big Dipper pointing the way to Polaris, the North Star. Hang on to it. We'll use it soon.

Did you know? Polaris is not the brightest star in the sky. It ranks only around 48th. It's famous for where it sits, not for how bright it is.

2.text:
Why Does the Moon Change Shape?

Every month the Moon goes from a thin sliver to a big round disk and back again. You've seen it happen your whole life. But what is actually going on up there?

Here are three ideas. A) Earth's shadow covers part of it. B) Clouds or dust block part of it. C) We see different amounts of its lit half.

Vote now, before we find out. Pick one and commit, because you'll get to test your answer yourself with a lamp and a ball later in this deck.

3.text:
Today I Can...

Here's where we're headed. Copy these into your notebook as "I can" statements so you can check yourself at the end.

I can use Polaris to find my latitude. I can explain the seasons with Earth's 23.4° tilt. I can explain the Moon's phases and why eclipses are rare. And I can explain daily tides, plus the bigger spring tides and smaller neap tides.

That's a full night's worth of sky for one lesson. Keep the list handy, because you'll rate yourself 1 to 3 on each one when we finish.

4.text:
Part 1: The Sky Above

Imagine lying on your back in a dark field far from town. What shape does the sky seem to be? Most people say a dome, like a huge bowl turned upside down over them.

Now add the half of the sky hidden below the ground, and you've got a whole ball surrounding Earth. Every star looks equally far away, as if someone painted them all on the inside of that ball. In this part we'll learn to use that ball as a map.

5.text:
The Celestial Sphere

The celestial sphere is an imaginary ball of sky around Earth. It isn't a real shell. It's a model of how the sky looks, and astronomers still use it as their map of the sky today.

A few points on this ball are worth knowing. The north celestial pole (NCP) sits right above Earth's North Pole, very close to Polaris. The south celestial pole (SCP) sits above the South Pole. The celestial equator is Earth's equator projected out onto the sky, like a giant hoop around us.

One problem: the stars are not really all the same distance away. Proxima Centauri is about 4.2 light-years from us, while Deneb is somewhere around 1,500 to 2,600 light-years away (its exact distance is hard to measure). Our eyes just can't sense the difference, so the sky looks like a smooth dome. The ancient Greeks, and later Ptolemy, thought the sphere was a real crystal shell carrying the stars. New observations in 1838 showed the stars sit at different distances, but the model still works fine as a map.

Did you know? For your own spot on Earth, the point straight overhead has a name: the zenith.

6.text:
Constellations

There are exactly 88 official constellations. You might picture a constellation as a connect-the-dots drawing, but officially it's a region of the sky, like a state on a map of the United States. Every star belongs to exactly one.

The International Astronomical Union adopted the official list in 1922 and fixed the borders in 1930. On this map you can see Ursa Major, the Great Bear, marked out as one region.

The stars in a constellation usually have nothing to do with each other. They just happen to lie in the same direction from Earth. Some could be close to us and others much, much farther back.

Did you know? Free apps like Stellarium Web can show you exactly which constellations are over your town tonight.

7.text:
Asterisms

An asterism is a familiar star pattern that isn't an official constellation. The most famous one in Indiana is the Big Dipper. It's made of seven bright stars sitting inside the constellation Ursa Major, the dashed region on the slide. So the Big Dipper is the picture, and Ursa Major is the whole neighborhood around it.

Other asterisms include the Summer Triangle, made of the bright stars Vega, Deneb, and Altair, which come from three different constellations, and Orion's Belt. And just like constellations, these patterns are usually not real groups. The Big Dipper's stars range from about 80 to 125 light-years away.

Here's a handy trick. The two stars at the end of the Dipper's bowl, Merak and Dubhe, point straight to Polaris. Follow them about five times the gap between them, and there's the North Star.

Did you know? From northern Indiana, the Big Dipper never sets. It circles the North Star all night, every night of the year. From Vincennes, only the tip of its handle dips just below the horizon for a short time.

8.text:
Diurnal Motion

Diurnal motion is the sky's daily turn. It looks like the stars are moving, but they're not. Earth spins from west to east, so the whole sky seems to turn the other way. That's why the stars, the Sun, and the Moon all rise in the east and set in the west.

Face north at night and you'll see the stars circle counterclockwise around Polaris. Polaris itself barely moves, because it sits within about 0.7° of the north celestial pole. It's like the hub in the middle of a spinning wheel.

Stars close to Polaris never dip below the horizon at all. These are called circumpolar stars. From Vincennes, at 38.7° N, any star within about 39° of the pole stays up all night long.

Did you know? The stars come back to the same spot every 23 hours and 56 minutes, not 24 hours. So each star rises about 4 minutes earlier every night, and that's why the constellations shift with the seasons.

9.text:
How Fast the Sky Turns

The sky makes one full turn, 360°, in about 24 hours. Divide it out: 360 ÷ 24 = 15. So the sky turns 15° every hour.

Look at the diagram. It's like a 24-hour clock face wrapped around Polaris. Each tick is one hour of the sky turning, and the yellow wedge shows one hour's worth: 15°.

You can measure this with your own hand. At arm's length, your fist covers about 10°. So every hour, the stars slide about one and a half fists around the North Star.

Did you know? Photographers leave their cameras open for hours to catch "star trails," curved streaks that show this turning. The longer the trail, the longer the camera was open.

10.text:
Polaris and Latitude

Here's one of my favorite tricks in this whole course: the altitude of Polaris equals your latitude. Measure how high the North Star sits above your northern horizon, and you know how far north you are on Earth.

This works because Polaris sits almost exactly above Earth's North Pole. Stand at the North Pole (90° N) and it's straight overhead. Stand on the equator (0°) and it sits right on the horizon. In between, it climbs 1° for every 1° you travel north. In Vincennes, IN, at 38.7° N, Polaris sits about 39° above the northern horizon.

Indiana runs from about 37.8° N at the Ohio River to 41.8° N at the Michigan line, so Polaris is 38° to 42° up everywhere in the state. That's about four fists above the horizon. Sailors used this exact trick to find their latitude for centuries.

Did you know? If you lived in the Southern Hemisphere, you couldn't see Polaris at all. It would always be below your horizon.

11.text:
The Ecliptic

As Earth travels around the Sun, the Sun seems to drift slowly against the background stars, about 1° a day. Over one year, it makes a full loop around the sky. That yearly path is called the ecliptic, the orange wave on the slide.

The ecliptic is tilted 23.4° to the celestial equator, the dashed line. That's because Earth's axis is tilted by the same amount. In June, the Sun sits 23.4° north of the celestial equator. In December it sits 23.4° south. At the two equinoxes, it crosses right over it.

Read the names along the wave: Pisces, Aries, Taurus, Gemini, Cancer, Leo, Virgo, Libra, Scorpius, Ophiuchus, Sagittarius, Capricornus, and Aquarius. These are the constellations the Sun passes through. Count them up. We'll talk about that number next.

Did you know? The planets and the Moon always stay close to the ecliptic too, because our solar system is nearly flat, like a pizza.

12.text:
The Zodiac

You've probably heard there are 12 signs of the zodiac. But using the official constellation borders set in 1930, the Sun's yearly path actually passes through 13 constellations, not 12.

The 13th one is Ophiuchus, the Serpent Bearer. The Sun is in Ophiuchus roughly from November 29 to December 17. Since the planets and the Moon stay near the ecliptic too, you'll always find them in or near these 13 constellations.

One more twist: when the Sun is "in" a constellation, you can't see that constellation, because it's daytime! At midnight you see the one on the opposite side of the sky.

Did you know? Astrology's 12 signs don't match the real constellations anymore. They've drifted about a month off since they were named around 2,000 years ago. Astrology has no scientific support. Astronomy is the science.

13.text:
Check for Understanding: Fort Wayne

Time to use your new trick. In Fort Wayne, Polaris sits 41° above the northern horizon. What is Fort Wayne's latitude?

Is it A) 41° N, B) 49° N, C) 23.4° N, or D) you need a telescope to know?

Look back at Slide 10, choose one, and be ready to explain why the other three don't work.

14.text:
Part 2: The Sun's Year

Quick poll before we start: raise your hand if you think Earth is closer to the Sun in summer. Lots of hands usually go up. Keep your answer in mind, because this part might surprise you.

We're going to follow the Sun through its yearly cycle: the seasons, the longest and shortest days, and the moments when day and night are about equal. Then we'll ask a strange question: is the North Star going to be the North Star forever?

15.text:
Seasons

Earth's axis is tilted 23.4°, and that tilt, not our distance from the Sun, is what causes the seasons. The axis keeps pointing the same direction in space, toward Polaris, all year long. So for half the year the Northern Hemisphere is tipped toward the Sun, and for the other half it's tipped away.

Being tipped toward the Sun does two things. First, sunlight hits the ground more directly. Look at the slide: in summer, a direct beam makes a small, bright patch. In winter, the same light comes in slanted and gets spread out over a bigger area, so each spot gets less warming. Second, the days get longer. Indiana gets about 15 hours of daylight in June but only about 9½ hours in December.

Want proof that distance isn't the cause? Earth is actually closest to the Sun, about 147.1 million km, around January 3, right in the middle of our winter. It's farthest, about 152.1 million km, around July 6.

Did you know? Earth's tilt isn't fixed forever. Over about 41,000 years it slowly rocks between about 22.1° and 24.5°, and that helps set the timing of ice ages. You'll see this again in Q2.

16.text:
Solstices and Equinoxes

A solstice is the day the Sun reaches its farthest point north or south, 23.4° from the celestial equator. An equinox is when the Sun crosses the celestial equator, and day and night are roughly equal everywhere, about 12 hours each.

Here's the 2026 calendar for Indiana, with how high the noon Sun climbs in Vincennes. The March equinox is March 20, with the noon Sun about 51° up. The June solstice is June 21, when the Sun hits its highest, about 75°. The September equinox is September 22, back to about 51°. The December solstice is December 21, when the noon Sun sits lowest, only about 28°.

You can figure these out yourself. At the equinox, the noon Sun's height is 90° minus your latitude: 90 − 38.7 = 51.3°. Add 23.4° for June and subtract 23.4° for December. Notice the Sun is never straight overhead anywhere in Indiana. That only happens between the Tropic of Cancer and the Tropic of Capricorn.

Did you know? The June solstice isn't the hottest day of the year. The hottest weeks come about a month later, because oceans and land take time to warm up.

17.text:
Precession

Have you ever watched a spinning top start to lean? Its axis slowly circles around in a cone. Earth's axis does the same thing, just way slower. One full wobble takes about 26,000 years. This is called precession.

The tilt stays about 23.4°, but the direction the axis points slowly traces a big circle across the sky. The cause is gravity: the Sun and Moon tug on Earth's bulging middle (Earth is about 43 km wider at the equator than from pole to pole), and because Earth is spinning, that tug makes the axis wobble.

That means the North Star changes! Right now it's Polaris. Around AD 14,000, about 12,000 years from now, the axis will point near Vega instead. And when the Egyptian pyramids were built, around 2700 BC, the pole star was Thuban.

Did you know? The Greek astronomer Hipparchus discovered precession around 130 BC by comparing his star positions with records made about 150 years earlier. New data changed the old idea of a fixed sky.

18.text:
Check for Understanding: No Tilt?

Here's a thought experiment. Picture Earth with a 0° tilt, its axis standing straight up and down as it goes around the Sun. Compare it with the real Earth and its 23.4° tilt on the slide.

Would we still have seasons? Why or why not?

Think on your own for a minute, then share with a partner. Look back at the flashlight beams on Slide 15 before you decide.

19.text:
Part 3: The Moon

Have you ever seen the Moon in the daytime? Most people have, and it's worth remembering. Hold on to that observation, because it's going to help you settle the vote from Slide 2.

The Moon's orbit explains three things we see from Earth. Its phases follow a 29.5-day cycle. Its eclipses are rare, because its orbit is tilted 5°. And its pull shapes the tides, with bigger and smaller tides that follow the phases. Let's take them one at a time.

20.text:
Moon Phases

A phase is how much of the Moon's lit half we can see. Start here: the Sun always lights up half of the Moon, the half facing the Sun. As the Moon orbits Earth, we get a different view of that lit half.

Follow the diagram. At new Moon, the Moon sits between Earth and the Sun, so its lit side faces away from us and we can't see it. A week or so later, at first quarter, we see half the disk lit. At full Moon, it's on the far side of Earth from the Sun, so we see the whole lit face. Then comes third quarter, and back to new. One full cycle takes 29.5 days, and Earth's shadow is not involved at all.

The Moon also spins exactly once each time it orbits, so we always see the same face. But there's no permanent "dark side." Both sides get about two weeks of daylight and two weeks of night.

Did you know? On a thin crescent Moon, you can sometimes see the dark part glowing faintly. That's earthshine: sunlight bouncing off Earth and lighting up the Moon.

21.text:
Activity: Lamp and Ball Moon

Time to test your vote from Slide 2. A lamp is the Sun, so turn the room lights off. A ball on a pencil is the Moon, and your head is Earth.

Hold the ball at arm's length, a little above your head, and turn slowly to your left. Stop at 8 places around the circle and sketch the lit part of the ball each time. Find the spots where it looks full and where it looks new.

But predict first. Where will the ball be when it looks full? And does your head's shadow make the phases? Write down your predictions before you start turning.

22.text:
Eclipses

An eclipse happens when the Sun, Earth, and Moon line up exactly. There are two kinds. In a solar eclipse, the new Moon passes right between the Sun and Earth, and the Moon's shadow falls on Earth. In a lunar eclipse, the full Moon passes into Earth's shadow, and it often turns a coppery red from sunlight bent through Earth's atmosphere.

Shadows have two parts. The umbra is the full, dark shadow, where you get a total eclipse. The penumbra is the lighter outer shadow, where the eclipse is only partial. The diagrams on the slide aren't to scale, but they show who blocks whom.

Total solar eclipses can happen thanks to that lucky match from Deck 1: the Sun is about 400 times wider than the Moon but also about 400 times farther away. On April 8, 2024, a total solar eclipse crossed southern and central Indiana, including Vincennes, Bloomington, and Indianapolis.

Did you know? Around 350 BC, Aristotle argued that Earth is round because its shadow on the Moon during lunar eclipses is always curved.

23.text:
Why Eclipses Are Rare

If a new Moon passes between the Sun and Earth every month, why don't we get an eclipse every month? The answer is one small number: 5°. The Moon's orbit is tilted about 5° compared to Earth's orbit around the Sun.

Look at the side view. Most months, the full Moon slides just above Earth's shadow, and the new Moon slides just below the Sun. They miss the exact line. An eclipse can only happen when a new or full Moon lands near one of the two spots where the Moon's orbit crosses Earth's orbit plane. Those spots are called nodes.

The lineup only comes around in about two "eclipse seasons" a year. That's why every year has at least 2 solar eclipses, but never more than 7 eclipses in all, counting solar and lunar together.

Did you know? Eclipse patterns repeat about every 18 years and 11 days, a cycle called the Saros.

24.text:
Check for Understanding: Which Phase?

Picture the Sun, Earth, and Moon from the last two slides. A lunar eclipse needs Earth's shadow to land on the Moon.

So which Moon phase can have a lunar eclipse? Is it A) new, B) first quarter, C) full, or D) third quarter?

Sketch the Sun, Earth, and Moon if it helps, pick your answer, and be ready to explain why the other three can't work.

25.text:
Tides

If you've spent a day at the beach, you've watched the water creep up the sand and then slide back. Most coastlines get two high tides and two low tides every day. The Moon's gravity is behind it.

The trick is that the Moon pulls harder on the side of Earth closer to it and more weakly on the far side. That difference stretches Earth's oceans into two bulges: one facing the Moon, and one on the opposite side. The low tides sit in between. (The bulges on the slide are exaggerated so you can see them.)

Earth spins under those bulges. But the Moon is also moving along its orbit in the same direction, so a spot on Earth needs about 50 extra minutes to catch back up to it. That makes one tidal day 24 hours 50 minutes long, with high tides about 12 hours 25 minutes apart.

Did you know? Real tides depend on the shape of the coast. The Bay of Fundy in Canada has tides about 16 m high, while Lake Michigan's tides are less than about 5 cm.

26.text:
Spring and Neap Tides

The Sun raises tides too, but its effect is a little less than half of the Moon's (about 46%). The Sun has about 27 million times the Moon's mass, but it's also about 390 times farther away, and tides weaken very fast with distance: twice as far means only 1/8 the tide. Its huge distance almost cancels out its huge mass. When the Sun and Moon team up, or work against each other, the tides change.

A spring tide happens when the Sun and Moon line up, at new Moon and full Moon. Their bulges add together, so you get the highest high tides and the lowest low tides: the biggest tidal range. A neap tide happens at the quarter Moons, when the Sun and Moon are at 90° to each other. Their pulls partly cancel, so the range is small.

Spring tides have nothing to do with the season. The name comes from water "springing up." They happen twice a month, all year, about every 14.8 days.

Did you know? "Neap tide" doesn't mean low tide. It means a small difference between high and low.

27.text:
One Face Forever

Ever notice that the Moon always shows us the same face? That's not a coincidence. Earth's tidal pull slowly braked the Moon's spin until one side always pointed toward us.

This is called tidal locking. The Moon now spins exactly once for every one trip around Earth. Picture walking in a circle around a friend while always facing them: by the time you get back to the start, you've turned all the way around once.

Our Moon isn't alone. Most major moons in the solar system are tidally locked to their planets.

Did you know? Pluto and its moon Charon are locked to each other, so each one always shows the other the same face.

28.text:
The Moon Is Drifting Away

The Moon is slowly moving away from us, about 3.8 cm farther every year. That's about how fast your fingernails grow.

It comes back to the tidal bulge. Earth spins once a day, while the Moon takes 29.5 days to go around. So Earth's fast spin drags the bulge a little ahead of the Moon. That bulge tugs the Moon forward, nudging it into a slightly bigger orbit, year after year.

Run the clock backward and the young Moon was much closer. Models estimate the newly formed Moon was about 20,000 km away, almost 20 times closer than today's 384,000 km.

29.text:
Your Turn: Tide Model

Now you're the scientist. You'll draw two frames: one for a spring tide and one for a neap tide. In each frame, the Sun and Earth are already in place.

Your job is to draw the Moon where it belongs, sketch the two tidal bulges, and label high and low tide. Then name the Moon phase in each frame.

Look back at Slides 25 and 26 if you get stuck. Finish with one sentence: "Spring tides happen at ___ because ___."

30.text:
Exit Ticket

You covered a lot of sky today. Show what you've got with three quick questions.

First, explain the Moon's phases without using Earth's shadow. Second, why don't we get a solar eclipse at every new Moon? Third, there's a full Moon tonight. Will we have spring or neap tides this week, and why?

When you're done, flip your card over and rate yourself 1 to 3 on each "I can" statement from Slide 3.

31.text:
One More Question

Here's a bonus question to stretch your thinking. Why do we always see the same side of the Moon?

The catch: your answer has to use the word tides. Look back at Slide 27 and give it a try.

32.text:
The Standards Behind This Lesson

This lesson follows the Indiana Earth and Space Science standards. Here's what they ask you to do, in plain words.

ES.4.7 is the main one: make diagrams or models showing how the Sun's and Moon's gravity pull on Earth's oceans, explain the difference between daily tides (high and low) and monthly tides (spring and neap), and explain how the monthly tides follow the Moon's trip around Earth, and so its phases.

Two more get a first look here. ES.4.6 is about the difference between weather and climate, and how slow changes in Earth's tilt (obliquity), the wobble of its axis (precession), and the shape of its orbit (eccentricity) helped cause ice ages over thousands of years. You'll dig into that in the Q2 climate deck. ES.2.5 is about how science changes as new observations come in, from Ptolemy to Copernicus, Brahe, Kepler, and Galileo. That's the whole story of Deck 3, "From Ptolemy to Newton."
